turns.prompt:
You are given two attached CSV files:
  - cdft_topo_sp_eg_train.csv: 200 crystalline materials, columns `formula`,
    `poscar` (the crystal structure, in POSCAR format), `spillage` (the
    spin-orbit spillage, dimensionless) and `band_gap` (the band gap, in
    eV).
  - cdft_topo_pool.csv: 100 CANDIDATE crystalline materials whose properties
    are NOT given, columns `candidate_id`, `formula` and `poscar` (the
    crystal structure, in POSCAR format).

Using the training data, select the 5 candidates with the LARGEST spin-orbit
spillage that also satisfy a bulk-gap requirement: the band gap must be at
least 1 eV. Band gaps are NOT given for the pool -- you must infer them. A
selected candidate whose band gap is below the threshold scores zero.

Reason from the structures, then end your answer with an explicit ranked
list of candidate_ids, best first, e.g. "Final: c901, c902, c903, c904,
c905".
turns.answer_text:
The training set shows that spillage values of order 1–2 occur only when strong SOC (heavy 5d/6p atoms) produces band inversion. Almost all such cases are metals (gap = 0). The rare exceptions that simultaneously satisfy gap \(\ge 1\) eV are closed-shell, anion-rich compounds (LiMgBi, HoS, Ga\(_3\)Os, TeI\(_2\), ThSe\(_2\), \ldots).  

Consequently the pool was screened first for charge-balanced, anion-rich compositions (oxides, iodides, bromides, pnictides) that contain Bi, Ir, Te, I or Tl, then ranked by the expected strength of inversion. Molecular/ionic crystals of the heaviest p-block elements and isolated 5d octahedra are the closest analogues to the gapped high-spillage training examples and are therefore expected to remain insulating while still producing sizable spillage.

Final: c048, c046, c039, c093, c097
